blocks.x: Okay, it's January 14th. We're at 195 West 10th Street and I'm talking to Ed Allen. Now Ed, the only thing I know about your early career is what it says on the back of this record. You were born in Nashville, Tennessee, December 15th, 1897. Is that right? Yeah, that's right.

And what about you folks? Were they interested in music at all? No, my mother played a little ear piano, but I'm not the only one who came up for me. I used to play on the beat on the table with my fingers and so forth, so she said, I'm going to give you some lessons. In fact I took piano lessons for about six months until the kids started a kid band running up by the street in St. Louis and I wanted to know how they were playing on piano. At that time a man played a piano, a boy playing piano called him a sissy. So I wanted to blow a horn and so the kid band, my mother put up in the kid band, I forgot all about piano there. When did you first start to play the trumpet? I was about 1916. I first started on a bugle. Did you have any teachers?
Yeah, we had a band teacher. Yeah, good, it's picking it up. I wasn't sure if it was getting it. You had a teacher for your band, what did you have, a little kid band?

Well we had a kid band, but then we started from kids, but we were in the range until some of them up in the 20s before that. Colonel, who was at them, was not a pitching band, an organization band, see? And we played for, we weren't allowed to play military music. And we had a fellow named Thorn Blue, a clinic, I guess you know him. His father used to teach us. He was a wonderful trumpet player. And that old lady called him cornet. And he was our first teacher teacher in the group. But coming up in the group I was a little faster than others, so I used to help the others. I was under a trumpet player after him along until we got further advanced. So we had rehearsal once a week, Thursday night, and then on Tuesday night we had rehearsal just about seven, we'd just do what we could ourselves until Professor Blue was able to come around in Thursday. Did you get any jobs with this little band? Did you get regular work? Well we used to play concerts once, say two or three concerts a year during the winter season. See this band was a military band, we had from 20 to 35 musicians there. But then the dance, a few of them were a little faster than others, we used to already have a little dance group. We didn't have no piano, so we'd have a drum, a couple of trombones, saxophone and clarinet, and go out and play dances.
So you were playing professionally about what year? Well professionally I would say back

I was 18, 19, 18, because I used to play with a three piece group out in a roadhouse, go out on the outskirts of St. Louis and play in what we call nightclub, roadhouses, and have piano, drums, and trumpet. That day there was a bunch of them saxophone, saxophone was just coming through then. Did you ever play with clarinet? Not often because clarinet players were very slow in that day. They didn't have too many clarinet players in St. Louis? No. We had some in the band. Thornton Blue was one of the best clarinet players in those days, Professor Blue's son.
Did you ever get outside St. Louis in those years to play? Did you get jobs on the road?

No, not until I left St. Louis. During those years, before I left St. Louis, I would do some work. I married young, so I had to work. I didn't labor and work, packing house. I did work in the foundry. I played a lot in the nightclubs, two and three nights a week out on the outskirts. But after I left St. Louis in 1920 I went out on the coast, Seattle. And I've been playing music ever since. I went out that state about two years, played on the nightclub. A fellow came to St. Louis and wanted some musicians. I went from Forbes. Went from there. Went out to Seattle, Washington, I forget the nightclub. What kind of music were you playing? Did you have written music at all or was it all by ear? Well, no, we weren't allowed to play by ear. We picked that up ourselves. All the musicians, you take all the musicians and they liked to pick the band and the band. And we had to read. We played all the old and concerts and everything. Military music. We had marches like down the funeral. We played military marches and funeral marches. If you couldn't read, Professor Blue didn't want to be bothered. He taught you how to read. That was the first thing. So we did more reading than we could think in those days. So if you didn't read, we caught it. You'd give a listen to read. You're going to play it when you come back. You want to know why. Well how about the little three or four piece bands? Well by orchestrating we played there. The majority of us played. Maybe with a little band like that? Yeah. We played by orchestration downtown. We used to have two trumpets, a trombone, a bass, never had any string at all. We played jobs, regularly. We played carnivals. The band is a whole weeks ago we played for the churches, have bazaars during the bazaar season. We played many friends for them and we'd go out and play the whole night. We had to pay for it too. How old were you then? You were a little then. Well at that time I must have been in my late teens. Because I was about twenty when I left St. Louis to go out on the coast. And since then I've been playing beauty for my living. I had no other job since then. No other job since then? No. Well that's wonderful. But before then I did little everything I was, as I said before, it's now I married a young I had to do some work. I had to do some work. I had to do some work. I was in the packing house. I drove a laundry truck. All this from the young boy up. So that's when I ran off me a job to go out on the west. I think it was a guarantee of fifty dollars a week. And that was a whole lot of money. It was a fifty dollars a week. I had to buy. So we grabbed it. We were all from St. Louis. And I went out there and made good and everything since then I've been doing something. And when I came back there I went on, I worked in a little nightclub in St. Louis during the winter season. Stratford came out there and wanted a group to go on the boat in the daytime around the St. Louis day ride. We had a plan of presence I was working with. And we all got six pieces we played in the day boat every day. Well nine o'clock in the morning until five Friday night. But I never preached most of the picnics.
And what kind of music did you play? How was the actual music you played? Was it Bahia or

Red Music? No it was not music. The average musician on the same list never played Bahia. He didn't? Well he learned that along with his music. But as a musician could read. And to play a job like on the boat around you had to read something. Now we had a regular station around every week and he'd start playing all the street and played pop music. And after I got Mr. Treckfuss he gave the music. He'd see jazz music every week. Well that summer I worked on the boat all that summer in St. Louis with a guy named Costello, kind of a band. Where did the boat go? It only went up so many miles. It was just a picnic like. Well out from the levee up to the river maybe three or four, five miles. And the Lord around the middle of the river until we made five o'clock and come back. We used to about five, five, there was all from school, picnics, and children. We had to get kids out for holidays. So during that season, St. Louis wanted another band. The St. Louis had a band down in the winter every year, down in New Orleans. So during that summer, St. Louis wanted a band, a different band. So he picked the man he wanted from, he had a group on the night go to St. Paul, we were out there in the daytime. And I think he had another boat that had, yeah, St. Louis was on there. So he picked a band called the Gold Whistler Band and called me in the office and said, I like your work and I'm organized a lot, I want a band to go down, you want to go down here? I thought that was great, I never had a band before. So he got put us, he called Eddie Allen Gold Whistler Band. What was the name now? Eddie Allen and the Gold Whistler Band. Gold Whistler Band. Yeah, we didn't have to play too loud. About how old was he when you had the band? Well, let's see, I can go back those days. I'd say I was about 24, 25, somewhere in there, because after I came back from the coast, and I went out on the coast when I was 20, 21. And I came back to San Luis during this winter season after I make this following summer on the boat. He picked out Casey, Florida Casey, on the Washington Wood Records, myself, Gene Cedric, Mason on alto, Gene Cedric, great tenor, and Pop Foster was on the bass, I guess you've heard a lot about him. At least from New Orleans. Yeah, from our very good friend. He was playing bass and his brother was playing band, George Foster. But before George Foster, Johnny Cedric played. Well you had a lot of New Orleans fellas then? Yeah, most of them was from New Orleans, except the boys from St. Louis. He picked these men out he wanted for this band, the sons down to New Orleans. He put me in charge of 80 hours, and he goes to the band. And we did some good work down in New Orleans. We had something good, we didn't have since nothing of it. Well you had a lot of competition there too. Yeah, well we were, at that time, I don't remember exactly, but all the hotels and the dancing was sending the musicians down to the capital steam to see what was happening all day.
It was a talk of the time. They'd come out and see what that band was playing. Well what did the band sound like? Was it like Dixieland today would you say?

Well it was a higher form because the first time wasn't usually then, had three reeds. See we had three reeds, three brass and four rhythm. Well that was a big band for those years. I was a big band. That's what I said. It was the first time to have a big band like that. And it was somewhat unusual. And we'd get to rehearsal and we'd say we were going to play this, and we had our own head arraignment and Mason because we met, what we were going to play, he'd write out, we'd get together and we were going to play this and play that. And we'd get on the night on the job, it sounded so good, the captain always going to say, what is that? Well we said something we had to give up, keep that in. I'll never forget we played one of New Orleans' favorite, I can't think the name of it now, but we made it up and made another arrangement and all that, practically a head arrangement. And it went so great that we used to rock the boat when we played it, Captain Joe used to come up and tell us, don't play that no more. And if we wouldn't play it again, if we'd stop and raise so much noise, he'd come up and say, hey, let's play that again, just play it and
then go into something else. I can't think of any of that number. It's one of New Orleans'
standard numbers. Is it like a march or something?
No, not that. Panama. Yeah. Is that Panama?

That particular one, we got that set together on with what you call a head arrangement, we play this and you play that and I play this. It sounds so good but it's different from what they've been hit in New Orleans, all the New Orleans music, but with a large ten piece band and playing that they ain't never heard before, we made a big hit.
Well that must have been one of the first big bands like that around the time.

We started a jazz band, a swing band. But we came back in St. Louis in the summer, that following summer we worked in St. Louis on jazz and I'd go first out in the color band on that. And we took the city, came back home and took the city by Star.
Well that was in the very early 20s. Yeah, that was early, early.
But that's the star of the alto. Used to use the C-mallure saxophone those days.
Do you remember any musicians in New Orleans that were particularly good?

There was a trumpet player that I had called Kid Punch. I don't know how to grow him. I knew a very bunch of musicians that I had forgotten. And then Kid, it seemed like the old name, Kid something. I had forgotten. I used to hang out with a bunch of them. I don't remember now, it's been so many years ago. You thought Punch was good on trumpet? Yeah. I always admired the trumpet players in New Orleans. I only had the swing. I always liked the swing. The majority didn't do much reading in New Orleans but they could play it. Like Johnny Sensen said, George Foster on the guitar after Johnny Sensen said, Johnny Sensen said was one of the first time I'd seen a guy play a six-strain band. It sounded so good, it was great. I don't remember the piano player we had. I don't remember the piano player we had. We had this boy Floyd Casey. He was a drummer. He picked up San Luis.
He goes way back too. I didn't think he was that old.

Yeah. He was only about two years younger than I. I was born in December. He was about three years old. Three years at the most. Did you get to hear Oliver play in those years? Yeah, I used to marry Oliver and Louis Armstrong because when they came up to San Luis, that's before I worked on them both days. They used to come, all of us come to San Luis, the fake miracle. And Louis Armstrong was with him. And after that they went Chicago. That's why I had Gerald Book, both there and Louis and Oliver together doing duets. I never heard nothing
like that in all my life. It was so great. Well you played a lot with Oliver yourself later.

Well yeah, that was during the recording with Clarence Riggins, I came to New York. I met Oliver in Chicago when I went from that same place just visiting with a friend of mine. But I never did no playing with him until I came to New York and was doing work with Clarence Riggins.
Would you say your style was something like Oliver's?

Well some people say it. I don't know. I don't think so. But I hear on some records that they couldn't tell one from another. But I think it was different. I admire his style. But I thought it was different. But I heard several people say, you sound just like Joe Oliver. He made some records because I couldn't tell one from another. And I've made some records that were individuals by myself, one trumpet. And he made some with one trumpet, as they say with me on one record, and say to him on another. Which was the first band that you
would say that you played with that played what you could call jazz? Well this band, I can say this ten piece band. That was about the first one.

It was a real good band, real music. We had bands all over the country, because I remember what was going on. We just didn't have sense enough to procter by. We broke up the band, and we just didn't have the band. We broke up. How long did the band stay together? About two years. In fact, during the two summers, I was with Captain Joe, and demanded more money for the band. But as usual, that amount of money at that time was a lot of money for average musician, and he used to make that kind of money. So he didn't want to see it, and he signed, he went back and told me that the boys were satisfied, and I was going to want to score me. So he said, I'm going to give you a raise. I think you raised me fifty dollars. But the same band go back under Fayette Mariv was named. Fayette Mariv was named. Fayette Mariv was named. I went back to New Orleans and played about six months ago. I got this. No way at six months I played about three months ago, I quit and went to work in a nightclub down there.
Oh, right in New Orleans? Yeah.

Do you remember the name of the nightclub? It was Butchie, called Niggah Butchie. He had a nightclub on the corner next to Beansy. On one side it was a white club, and next door was a called Beansy club, he had a nightclub club there. Is that the fellow they call Beansy? I think he's still around. I don't remember. But this guy Butchie got me a job, he said, you don't want to, so many things, he said, you don't want to, how come you're not charged man, how come you got your band this year? I said, there's a whole lot of difficulty. He said, well if you don't want to work, you don't want to say anything, I want to give you a job. I thought it over, after a few hours, I was fading out of this lesson, I said, I think I'll quit. So I did quit. This guy gave me a job, he was paying the musician there, $25 a week, which was a good sign, but he said, I'll give you $40, you come and work, you have to come and work the restaurant, and this guy, and some of the other work, they started at 9 o'clock, I think, and I come around 10 or 11, and I leave for the, just the pressure that had been on the boat. But I stayed there until I gave a few lessons. He didn't want me to leave, he wanted me to stay there to make my home, and all of them, so I didn't want it. He said, I'll give you money, and get your mother, and that's why I got me to stay. I said, I did the same thing with Joe Oliver, and all of them used to work for me. But he didn't want me to leave, so I slipped off the left anyway.
Who was in the band? Who did you work with at the nightclub?

All I can remember is Julio O' Toms, a piano player, but I don't remember, he was the lead, but I don't remember the rest of the nightclub. You had a plan in that? I don't remember, it was about three or four pieces. A little band. I was a small group. I used to stay in the Beans' cabin when they wanted me to knock on the wall, told me to come on and play. At that time I'd been on the boat, and I had a little pressing, I didn't play, I didn't stay there and play, just told me the water be coming out. Maybe you'll play in this, back up. I'd be in the other place, having some fun with us. So he wanted me to stay the whole winter. I got disgusted and he tells me, I'm not going to let you go back so much, you've got to stay here. And after that time I was around the Fred and I was in South. The band started at nine o'clock and the train left at seven. So I used to take my horn and he said, hey, what you taking your horn on? I said, I've got to get some lessons. He didn't want me to take my horn on at night. I used to leave it in the bar. So I started taking my horn, I made plans to leave so I took my horn off about a month straight. So one night I caught the Panama and he looked for me to open up. I would have to be at ten or eleven o'clock, I was real on the way to St. Louis saying, I gave one back and then he'd go back to the other. And the funny thing about that, I was working at Cornish Inn in 1927 and 28. Cornish Inn was a very popular band those days. And I was in a band with Adderalls and Leroy and I was sitting there playing one night and this fellow Bootsy walked in. He looked
at me and he walked up and he said, you don't know me do you? I looked at him and I said, I've seen you somewhere. He said, I'm the guy you ran away and left down the road.

He said, I'm sure you ain't seen him. I'm glad to see you very good. I'm surprised I find you in New York. I was there about two years. So he gave the band a tip and water salt and drank. He said, this guy, he said, wait for me and he took the ring. He broke the way for me. I was looking for him to come to work 19 on the train going to St. Louis. You liked St. Louis better, huh? Well at that time, I didn't catch much of St. Louis. I was raised, I was home. So I'm glad to get away. I got away and stay here. Did you play a lot of blues on that job? Played on the boat? No, in your club? Yeah, blues, most of all they played, you know, style blues and swing music, what they call it, jazz over there. But in the band on the boat we played a little everything. Complete orchestration, arrangements. And we'd ask about to make arrangements for them. It sounds very good. It's so modern and different from what they've been here. It was the same thing put together but it put together better. And the jazz and all that combined, it was quite a hit. A lot of guys come to me on and say, why don't you guys go to New York, why don't you get somewhere else, so and so and so. I guess we didn't have sense of that. That was in the very early 20s.

Early 20s. Early 20s. I'd say about 24. I'm not, I'm not much unremembered big. Well they had a few big bands. I think Celestan had a big band by then. Yeah, they had seven pieces I think. Celestan, I've heard him record on the television,

the radio since I learned that. Celestan had a nice band since you mentioned it. I think he had seven, eight pieces. And then another guy that had trumpet playing, had a nice band. Yeah. Manuel Perez. Yeah. Manuel Perez. Man, that's the one. He's had a very nice band. I remember saying that when I was down, when I get old he was going over, I could continue to play, because at that time he must have been 40 or so. Was he that old then? I didn't know. Well that's what I think, because I remember saying he played so great, because he used to play opera on every Sunday. They used to run a high one of the local bands to play opera that's on a Sunday boat ride. And I heard he was going over and played so good, I used to sing, when I get old, you know, if I'd be able to play like him, but he'd still able to play. He was strong, was he? Yeah, strong, great. Very good trumpet playing. And his band was good too? And then we'll be like Celestine. What is Celestine? Celestine? Yeah, Celestine. Well he was on, he'd be on the books of silence too. They used local bands quite often for competition. How about Piran? Did you ever remember his band? No, I didn't remember his band. I met him in New York here I think.
You say you met Piran in New York? Yeah, two Clance Williams. Oh yeah, well they used to have a kind of a music business together.

Yeah, Clance Williams had a public company. I think he was connected, Piran was connected with us somewhere, I don't know. See when I come to New York I met Clance Williams and he had quite a few other fellows that I've heard of, either known or connected with him in the business, in his music game. Did you ever play with Clance Williams in New Orleans? No I didn't know him until I came to New York. I've heard of him. I think he was in Chicago for a great while. But I didn't know anything about Clance Williams no more about Reed or something, I heard of some of his music or something. When I came to New York I met him through Jasper Terra I think, with the drum along with the black and white band, I was with the Burleschio. And he knew Clance Williams. He said, well I'm not an officer, I'm not an officer, I'm not an officer, I'm a man-acquainted. And we're talking about his recording. He said, no, you boy, I'll give you a recording date. I said I can use three or four, I can use the whole band. And that's what my associate was from Ben Arden, he was with all his recordings. When I came back to live in New York, every time I put an email with the show, we'll do some recordings, it's a washboard band. That's four pieces. So when I came back, after I quit the road I called Clance Long Distance, I said did he have a recording. He said yes, come on, stay with me, I'm giving you a lot of work. So that's how come you stay in New York, I come on back from Cleveland. Oh, well how'd you get to Cleveland, now the last time?
Well I was with the show, I was traveling with the show. Oh I see. That was after you went back to St. Louis you got with the show.

No, after I went back to St. Louis, I worked in a night club there called Show for the Garden, for about, oh let's see, it was about a year or so. I was just getting up near 26 or 27, I was about to say about 25 when I was at St. Louis. I went to Chicago, someone called me to come to Chicago, to work at the night club there called the, after Oswald, I don't remember the real name of it, but that was the first time I ever met Earl Hines. He was there, had a band there five, six people, a friend of mine from St. Louis, but Chicago, the union wouldn't let them use a local musician. So a friend of mine called me from Chicago, come up there, said we need a trumpet player, but I think it's a local 208 in Chicago, wouldn't let them use a local musician, because Earl Hines and his group was from Pittsburgh, and they belong in that union. So they said they could call somebody until the time was up to get down the union. So that's how come they go to Chicago. I think it was called the E-Light Club, it was outside, so I didn't go to work until 12 o'clock, 1 o'clock, I worked until 1. And while I was sitting, I'll tell you how I got to New York now, while I was playing in this job, Joe Jordan come through, and one night, and they asked me how I'd like to go to New York. Well I'd never been to New York before, I was grabbing the check of the opportunity. So he said, well I'm expecting something, he says, I've got to make an audition for a burlesque show, would you be interested? I said, very much. So he said, come up to my house, and rehearsal, and this fellow come to, this fellow in office, if it's okay, you can go along. So I made rehearsal, and we didn't be in an audition to Steve in some theater down in Chicago, a loop, and the guy hired the band. And so he said, you're okay, he's gonna send us tickets in a week or so, and I'm sure what you did. And so he organized the band out of Chicago. But I was on one from St. Louis, but I was there, and so he liked it, and we went home, came on to New York, rehearsed the burlesque show. Yeah, the burlesque show, that's following September, somewhere, I don't remember even. Went on the burlesque show, you know, back to the same way to Chicago, Kansas City, Washington, Pittsburgh, and I was on that for two years. But each time I came to New York, I'd go to see Clarence Whitman, and we'd be playing around New York, because we'd be in New York sometimes for two or three weeks playing at New Jersey, New York, New York, Connecticut, and we'd run back in town to make some records. So we'd be a lot of watchful records. Months after releasing them, but they were made. So when the band, when the show broke out, the mix of August, I saw something, I don't know, earlier that, I either go back to St. Louis or Chicago, or I got to New York. So I'd be far to go to New York, and I called Clarence Whitman a long distance. But they had a car, he worked or something, he said, come on, I'll get you some work. So Casey was a drummer on this band too. So he and I picked up and came on New York, and I've been here ever since. And I worked, Clarence gave us plenty of work. That time he'd done several recordings a week. What about the regular work with Clarence? Did he have a regular job anywhere? No, he never had a regular job. Just recorded. I don't remember, it wasn't a steady job, it was a great record. But he had enough records. He made records for everybody, and all the records come to New York that time. I made records, and everyone, even the Edison at that time, and there wasn't a tickle about the jazz records, but we made a watchful records for everybody. And while I was making those, I had an opportunity to make an audition down to Conny then for a time to prepare me for leaving. A couple friends from St. Louis was in the band, and so I was in Conny. I made an audition with that at all, and I went down at stage two years.
The songs that Clarence Williams recorded were mostly his own songs?

Mostly all his own songs. So he'd make up some nights, we'd sit up and make them up overnight, but I'm going to make it. He said, Al, I got a record tomorrow. I said, what you're going to make? He said, I don't know. How does it sound? Blue, blue, blue, blue, blue. I said, sounds all right. He said, well, let's do the part. I'm going to make some more naked. I better make it with the next, put some name on it, and make it in the next three or four weeks, a month or two, he decided to publish it and put it out. A lot of the numbers came out months after, but he didn't record it. Put about a different name, but he can make it. He called me anything next morning, as long as I went on the record. Was he a good musician himself? Very good musician. He wasn't what you call a trained musician, he had a good ear, and he'd tell you when you're playing right and tell you when you're playing wrong. And he actually wrote down the numbers himself? No, he always had someone take them off, he'd play a number, take the melody, and he had the right harmony. Then make what you call a melody sheet for us, make a lead sheet. And get together and have somebody arrange for us. Most of the time with records, we'd be leading a lead sheet, we'd make up our own thing, just put it on tape, put it on the records. Didn't care what it was. Well, if it was a hit, popular number, he'd have an orchestration made for it. He'd have somebody on the street, have him play it up. And several of his numbers were that big. Did he have his own publishing company in those days? Yeah, he put the big, own books and everything. Big office staff, everything. First place music house. He's the president and everything, and I was a music company there. He had a big staff and everything.

Yeah. Secretary, arrangers, and he had different people coming in the range, like nobody else. You said he had somebody from his office that once made a record? Yeah, one time we had one of these things, I don't remember,

that's the number of records I've been trying to hear. I don't even understand his name. He was working his office, I don't know what he's done, any kind of office working on the secretary or something. He had a pretty nice voice. So the crime would take everybody, and take them down with Macon Carter. So it's at this point, he went on Thursday. He was saying on the other side his wife, even Taylor was saying. We made that for Bluebird, not Victor, that was a part of Victor. Subsidiar. Yeah. We made that record, and I've been trying to get that. That was a fair night. I can't even take the name. We might have that.
I'll have to look for it and see if I can find it. It's made around 1931 or 1932.

Very good record. Well that's a fairly late one though. Yeah. Eight piece banner. Eight piece banner. I can't even take the name of it. I'm going to look at the house when I go home. I might have it. I don't have it but there's one outside and I can't hear nothing in front of it. If I can find it I'll call you and give you the name. I'm going to look one day. Well they might have it in one of those books. Yeah. I don't remember seeing it in the jazz record I look for. I like that record very much. Was Floyd Casey on a lot of them with you? Yeah, Washboard with Floyd Casey, and Sister Scott, this boy St. Clair was on bass. I think the line played piano. Now a lot of dates we made, it was supposed to be Clarence rhythm was the line playing piano. See the line worked for the main record. Clarence played anybody, it was a long-nick record. Believe it or not, he said, Fat Wallace makes some records for Clarence. And the other Clarence were in there.
Would Clarence be there when the records were made?

Sometimes he'd be there but he would be playing. Fat Wallace played, the line played. And I tell you, he busted Bailey. And those fellas hadn't been in town with it. Particularly Fat Wallace had a little bit of a-
I know a whole lot of New Orleans fellas had numbers published by Clarence Williams that now belong to Decker. Yeah, that's right. Decker brought the whole catalog out.
And I understand that he gets a royalty from Decker and gets so much money from him. Yeah, he should. He should.
He probably does. Sure, any time one of his numbers comes out on the record, he's supposed to be paid royalty.

High Society, he got money from that picture, High Society. His number is in his catalog anyway, so he's published. He's got several numbers every time he calls. He gets something for it. So I would agree, but I'm calling him late.

I need to call him. I need to get a Christmas card. I'm not a hear from him. He's sick now. Yeah, he's sick. I'd like to talk to him myself, but I understand he's very sick. I don't know. You would get a Christmas card from him.
I didn't get one this year, so I imagine I'm going to call him. But he have a thrift shop on the thrift street. I've been that side. I've been there.
I saw his son there once.

Yeah. I hadn't seen him. I was a little kid, I wouldn't know him. I heard one of the police officers up in Connecticut, but the last time I've been two or three years I saw a guy and we had a long talk. And he was rehearsing some girl then, figuring he'd do his work for him. Really?
That was just a few years ago? A few years ago.

I had some girl, but he had a saint there for me. She was working in the store at the same time. Oh yeah? He still likes music though. Yeah, he still likes music. Like he told me, sure, a different day. He said a lot of people say I don't have no money and I don't have this. He said he was a good safe and show me and I'm doing all right. Well good, I'm glad to hear. Good to hear you. I'm glad to hear you. But every time one of my numbers come out I get something for her. I get too much money for the ticket, I guess, once a year or something like that. Was his wife still with him when you saw him? His wife was separated. He and his wife were separated at the time. But I've heard since then that they were planning to go back, but I don't know.
Really? Because she's been married to him since about 22 or something. I don't know.

It was married when I first came to New York. They had a nice home on the 36th and she was right there, but then we had a home out of Jamaica. Was she a good singer? Yes, very good singer. She was on, at that time used to be a band, I guess she was two years old, a band called a band of a thousand melodies I think. And she used to sing with everyone on the radio. Oh yeah, I didn't know that. She was a very good man for, I don't know, for two or three years. She was a good singer. She had a spot and then again she had a home spot on NBC. That wasn't jazz, that was a different kind of music. No, that's pop music. And she was sitting in a lot of spots like the half-landers and shows. That was a spot and she was very good. She had this program on Monday, every morning. I don't know what I'm doing at that. A band of a thousand melodies, that's what used to be. She was very good singer.
Now you were saying Clarence used to get his men from all over New York, huh? Anybody would come through? Yeah.

Anybody would come down. It's a lot of, everybody, even up to nine, the present day, the guy said, can you make a record for me? I want to record it. They want to do it. They asked them after the morning, then they asked to hear themselves play. I was speaking a lot of musicians now. They said, man I've never heard of them all. I've never heard the record, myself playing on record. Well that's unusual for the average guy. I said well you can go down and make a record if you want to hear yourself on that. But the average guy, he wants to say he made a record and he's got to pay for it. You know? Just like it's something you do. And when the Clarence asked me, do some recording? I said yeah, do some recording. That's a nice musician. Did you have a lot of music? I said, yeah, do some recording. That's a nice musician. Did you have a lot of fun in the sessions? Were they relaxed, would you say? Well not too relaxed. Some of them at that time kind of would let you relax.
No you wouldn't, huh?

We rehearsed here a long time, we get tired, we have a, I imagine the least of sessions are much more agreeable now in those days, the hard girl. Is that right? When you go down there in the water you didn't know what you were going to do. Either what you rehearsed to do or you go down and do just after. You rehearse this number, play this number, and the guy that don't like this number, even the record cutters, oh I don't like that Clarence, put something else in. You just spend all your time either at Nixon and I have to rehearse and the other sometimes you spend all your time so I'll have to rehearse. Then you've got to grab something else and rehearse that and make it rehearse it and make it all the same day, all that session. We don't have a morning session, a night session. One time he made a catalog with the, what do you call them? Piano Rolls, they went into the record business for a week. Yeah. For a week we was making catalogs, we went out there everyday and we got a catalog, QRX I think it was. How do you make a catalog? For a catalog, it's about to put some records out there, they had no records. Oh I see. So if you're going to put out some records, they have a Clarence Swing record, they have about to know his records. Somebody's going to be in that company, they're going to make a swimming record so that makes sure when they put their adverts out there they have a different sentence, I suppose it's called a catalog. I see what you mean. So we for a week we make up this catalog, I got a Clarence, I think about 15, 20, I was on there. We got some good money there because of the person, he was out there everyday. How long that lasts? At least I wasn't interested in how long that lasts, I get paid for the record. King Oliver was on some of those.
Yeah.

Well he was about anything class way man, King Oliver had something in there to do, he'd come to record it. Whenever he come in time, he'd make some recordings with his band. And most of the time King Oliver made his own band so he didn't have to have nobody. When Clarence was going to make something from his group, he'd set King in and all that. Always make some money see. Well Williams didn't have a regular group working anyway. No, I don't remember having a group in any spot at all. But most of the time he relied on his recording. Of course he didn't play that with everybody, record for everybody. Blues, singers and all. I'd like to tell you the other part of the first I taught them, there were contests all over the country, and they'd make the blues come and send a particular okay record. They'd come to New York's little wonder blues contest, but send them to New York to do the recording. And they'd call Glass and say, I got recorded, you know, I want to need a trumpet player, I need a piano player, you want to come out and play for this? He'd say, no, quite never, I got to turn it recording. I'd go out and make one record out of the room there. He said, I got recorded in the morning on a trumpet player, you want to go out and make it? I said, well yeah. I've made records I never heard of before, I'd never seen them. I'm going to go again about it. How they sound, good or bad, they'll pick a different out of the money. Well he certainly got good men. He always tried to get good men. Otherwise they would come back, if he got a recording, he didn't think it was good. He was that smart, he'd get somebody else. Next time, he'd call and so on and so on. He got them out of all the different bands. Different bands, different musicians in town. And he practically knew everybody. He even got them running by. Clarence got recorded, he was calling him Cuzz. Cuzz, what you got up? Can you go on some of your recording dates that they come up? You know something? He said, yeah, come on now, Cuzz. Come on, I got a date, so, so, so. He's going to give you a ring. He said, well, he said, we telegram. I wasn't living with him. He said, we telegram. I got recorded, text the date. Be down in the office or be down in the studio. So he text the date and we were all naked.

That's a good record. With whose band were you working at the time you made most of your recordings for Clarence Williams? Once I was working with Alain Rolf and Leroy Tiff, the band saved by Connie Zinn.
That was a Connie Zinn band. Yeah. Alain Rolf had a band first when he left, and Leroy Tiff took over. That was about three or two or three years later.
Where did Clarence Williams get the idea for the Washboard? That was his own idea, huh? I really think that was Jasper Taylor's idea, the drummer from Chicago.

He came in with us with this brother show I was telling you about. And I picked up a band, I picked up the New York with his band, and it seemed like he had did somebody call in or something out there in Chicago and he knew Clarence, so he went to Clarence and talked to everybody. It seemed like. So the first Washboard band, Jasper Taylor was playing the Washboard. And as we left, I don't remember why, we had another drummer. And then we got this fellow, Floyd Casey, and we told him I'd play the Washboard.
And we hadn't played it before?

No, he hadn't played it before. No, he hadn't played it before. I was actually here to him playing. I told him, I don't remember, Sam Wilson told him to make some money, he was featuring the Washboard then. So that's when he first started. It seemed like he'd be very good. Then Clarence, some of the records, Clarence's brother played the Washboard. He had a brother who just played the Washboard on Saturday. He wasn't the drummer, just the Washboard band? No, just Washboard band. But see on the Washboard, they made the Washboard band, you didn't have a job. In those days, they'd never used bass band, anyway, because the records wouldn't take it.
Did they ever use Washboards on a regular job in the evening? You mean on a steady job? Not as I knew of. I couldn't say yes or no.

But I do remember when we were on this Burles show, the band, we had a couple spots, I think it was Jack before he left, and he played a Washboard for a few bars instead of the spotlight for a Washboard and the rhythm would be playing or something like that.
Now the Connies Inn band, that was one of the best known bands in town?

Yeah, I wouldn't say the best known band, but it was one of the best known spots in town. Better raise your prestige when you worked at Connies Inn at that time. The Connies Inn Cotton Club up in Harlem, that was the Top Night Club. People come all over the world, they come here, Connies Inn and the Cotton Club. And that was in, what year, that was 27, 28, then the Top Night Club.
Was Ellington popular then, at that time?

It was just beginning. I guess Fletcher Henderson was more popular. Yeah, Fletcher Henderson was a band, he was like a rose band. Even before the Cotton Club got popular with the main bands they had in there. Did you ever play with Fletcher Henderson? No, I never had. I played some of his rings, but he used to play some of his rings down there and cut it in for us to play. I never played with him.
Do you remember when Perron's band came to New York? That was in the one of the band that came up there?

Yeah, but that was before I came to New York. That was before you came up there. Yeah. I remember reading about him. I remember Leroy Smith went to Carter then before Adam Ross, and he went back in there after the Art Tis came out. He went back in there. How about after you left the Cotton Museum? After I left the Cotton Museum, I went to do freelance gigging. I don't know who they were. I never heard the records before. I got paid for them. That's all I was interested. Well Willie the Lion Smith was one of them, huh? Yeah, well he went for Clarence too. Oh, he went for Clarence? He went for Clarence. I found that. I found that. He was a band. I found that a lot of numbers, Clarence, he worked for a band, and Willie the Lion, he played for Willie the Lion, he played for Willie the Lion, he played for many numbers. Clarence was so good he couldn't get it. I said, what you doing, Cos? I'm going to leave the card and be. But you know, okay, he's going to make it. Were there a lot of musicians from New Orleans in New York during these years?
I know a lot.
I think quite a few.
Were they good, would you say, as a rule?
You know there's nothing wrong with me, it shouldn't be very good.
It takes a little more than no arm struggle. How do you like Louise playing? Crazy about it. Crazy. Were you always crazy about it?
Yeah I'd stand on the boat before I did and say let's stand on the boat, let's make them play, and I'd play like that.

What were some of the other trumpet players you liked a whole lot? One boy from my home, Charlie Crick, I liked him great. Charlie who? Charlie Crick. Oh yeah I've heard of him. He played blues with him, beautiful tones. Did he ever record do you know?

I don't know. I think he recorded years in St. Louis. Okay people went around to different cities around that time and used to take their equipment and have their local fans record. I think he recorded a lot. And after he was in Chicago I don't know whether he didn't record or not. But at that time he was in St. Louis, he was very popular. He was a terrible trumpet player. Beautiful tone and he could play the blues. Did he use a mute? No he used to feature the dirt and most of them used to mute. He used to mute. Well that's what Oliver did too some, huh? Oh yeah.
Charlie had a movie called Gig, that's a gig band.

the suburb. He played. Sometimes he had two or three bands out at night. All around St. Louis and the suburb. Of course we were in Illinois. He was very great. People would all be great. Faith and Rival tour. Once you worked on the boat in St. Louis, Charlie and the Crest worked on, I worked with him on the boat for a short while in St. Louis. That empty Preston, St. Louis, the old days when people would all be called to get you. Freighted out, a great job. So I was expecting Friday, Saturday night. Is your trumpet style anything like Charlie Crest's? Somewhat. Some of the tones at that time, I don't know about, someone had some tones. You heard of Zooty Singleton? Well that's his wife, Charlie Pest's sister, his wife. And we were playing along for the end of St. Louis before we came to Easton. I was playing the job and his sister came by and I don't know somebody, I said look there there, I'm back there playing. She said that ain't Eddie, that's my brother, that's Charlie. And I just got a little further from the team and the people said come on, take me back, that's Eddie Adams playing. And at that time we played so much of life, especially in the tone. So she didn't want to believe it. So Charlie had a, we talked about it a long time, I said I don't want you around me but I'm playing.
I said I don't care. Was he about the same age as you are? I imagine so, I never even know exactly, I imagine so about the same age.
Is he still playing now is he? No he's dead now, he's been in suicide in Chicago at the same time.
In the 30s? Later than that, it wasn't the last 10 or 15 years.

Was he playing in recent years? I don't know. I don't know what he's done in Chicago. He's a guy, he couldn't play, he laid his horn down for three or four weeks a month, he doesn't play, you never tell the difference, he still plays. He'd pick up anybody on the horn and play. Bob Feele on the average trumpet player, can't use that right by a piece. But he couldn't pick up anything, he just blows. And when it blows, you knew about Charlie Crescent, you never seen him, you never heard that tone. Now I'm saying look, he was noted. He was here playing in the right area, we had to see him, not the last Charlie Crescent man.
Did you ever run into a trumpet player named George Mitchell? No I didn't. He was in Chicago all around I guess.

I stayed in Chicago about three months out of August. I was at the Eli Club, I was at the one I left there in the spring and joined the show. So I didn't meet too many musicians unless I lived by there from Chicago. I know quite a few musicians from Chicago but I didn't meet many around there.
Did you know any of the New Orleans musicians in New York? Well I guess Clarence Williams is really from there as well.

No I didn't know two men of them. Three men in that time didn't make them come this way. Both of them in Chicago. But I knew I was in Chicago and I knew I was in Chicago. I guess quite a few up here now but I don't remember.
So which bands did you play with in later years after Connie's in band? No regular band?

No, no regular band since I've been freelance. I played in several dance schools with different bands, no name bands. Just like I am now. I was like that band that wanted trumpet player, that wanted to play. In fact for a while I wouldn't take a cigar to put the band down to stage as a gig until I went there. I went last night. I figured when they were gigging I'd be playing one band at night and another tomorrow night. Anybody call me for a job. That job's pretty tiring, huh? Worse than that. That's mild. It's killing. But you say your lift is still in pretty good shape do you think?

Yeah, pretty good shape if I don't have to work too hard. I have a job for a safe instrument and a hard job to play with a big band. I don't think I can live now. Where I get four or five bands I got to pound out of it.

I can't play up high or I'm tired. I'm tired. I'm tired. I'm tired. I'm tired. I'm tired and play any kind of way. Just want to make the night. And I look at night and it's a nice work. And after you played two or three hours a year, you'll enjoy playing with them. Every day we played two or three hours a year. You'll enjoy playing with them. You play pretty good. You can't let yourself go. You let yourself go and play like you want to play or try and play like you want to play. But the four of the nights over here, you'll repeat it out. You never be playing up. Sometimes you get so tired that you go make a little bit and come out win. Oh yeah. Well I suppose this is bad when you have quite a few pieces as it is, just a four piece
proof. That must be really. Well four pieces.
Monday nights they're bad. That's terrible. You have to work so you make out with it. You have to pace yourself on the drums. They say the job's like that. It must be hard on Casey.
It must be hard on the drummer. Yeah. It's foot, drum and piano.

But it's not as hard as on a man blowing a horn. But people, a drum woman can pat his foot all night long. It's time up. But it's impossible for a man to blow a horn all night long. It's like on Monday nights we have four pieces. Time up, play a chorus, piano play a chorus, a saxophone play a chorus, and we all play a chorus together. But in other words I'm playing by every little chorus.
Every little chorus. That's terrible. It's too rough. So when you get tired you just go play any way you can and just make that night out.
Some nights might come there and the people out here, they say well I'm bad.
We're with them guys so I'm just trying to get that night through. I guess mostly everything you play there is pretty slow. Yeah mostly slow. That's the way the girls like it.

Yeah. For the purpose of 100% reason. So they've got to be slow. That's why we play some live numbers. The slow numbers are driving where you got it where you rip out too. Do they make much money in that place? They've got to make money. They pay off everybody. See, you know. Well if you figure you dance with four tickets for a dollar, then you get four courses for those four tickets. All we've got to do is have some people that, you can have four or five couples and they stay all night and they've got to make some money. You know you can't bang that long until you play four courses. You have to play a fast night and play two courses. Each two courses that's a ticket. That's 25 cents.
So are you a whole lot of people to pay off? All those girls and all the time you said that?
Yeah. Everything has to be paid. And this is what I recall you. Tell me later. Yeah.

But you say there's some good men in the band, huh? Rudy Powell, did he play clarinet too, was one of the sax? Yeah. He was a wonderful saxophone. He was one of our top saxophone players, believe it or not. You wouldn't think he'd be in a squad like that.

Oh no, that's a mess. And he's played with all the name bands, Fred Wallace, Capp, Calloway, every band band, he's been with them one time or another. Does he still play any clarinet? Yeah. Very good. He's very active too. Good musicians, great. Ranger and all. Writes and everything. He writes for some magazine in France, I think one in England too. A local durn over there.

Gee, he ought to be able to make some more recordings now. Yeah, he's getting along with it. What does he do when he makes a record? He takes the night off and pays somebody to come and make a play? Some of them come and work for him.
Sometimes this lady had a recording, God couldn't know what he did he got there. The last recording, he was lucky it was on Tuesday. That's his night off. He's one of our best saxophone players.
I don't believe that he would get as tired playing the sax as you would the trumpet. No.

Last time I'd be playing, he'd be playing, he'd pick up. He'd say, man I hear you live, I know you're tired, I'd make it out. He'd change us out for you, something like that. Did he play alto or tenor than I was in front of him and alto?

He had a tenor too though. Didn't I do that? I think so. But what's the leader play? The leader play piano. I don't think, I don't think. Well you had more than just the two horns, huh? Just the two of them. We had the tenor there, three pieces. We had three horns but the three pieces are only there on Wednesday, Friday, Saturday, and Sunday. I think I was there on Wednesday. I think I was there on Wednesday.

Well a full band was there, six pieces. Wednesday six pieces, Friday six pieces, Saturday and Sunday. But the other night we rotate, the men have the night off. Like on Monday the drummer and the tenor and the bass is off. On Tuesday the alto and the drummer is off. Wednesday the Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland outside the drum and the piano, we had no substitute for other bands. When the drum and the piano lost, they got the band in that place. But we don't get nobody for the other sports.
What did you say, that wasn't a second class job, it was a third class job? No, it wasn't that. It wasn't that. It was just a job, that's all.
Nothing to brag about.

Well at least you're working regularly. So few musicians are, especially the old timers. You think, well probably you and Rudy Powell, Floyd Casey, they play a lot of good old-time jazz too. Anybody want to hear it?

We're all up in the 80s except Newt, we've got a tenor player that's been in the last two months. I don't think he's 30 yet. But I think everybody else there is in the 50s. Is that right? I think Rudy was, the bass player, just hit 50 lately, between Rudy and me, but they're both in the 50s. So we said, you know, come down here, it's the 50, you can't wait. But the first we had on tenor that he's under 29, very good music, he's steady and hard. He wants to get out of there, huh? Well I guess we all do. But it's like the first of Saturday coming in. All the musicians loafing in New York now. It's nobody. Just a very few.
Well the guy at the Metropole seems to do pretty well I guess.

Well there's a few jobs always, but some of them just mean good money. And working life, working quite often, working steady. But I'm speaking of that as a whole. You've got to have a day job or something, some other rock of the summer to keep going. When you get a salary, they don't care how much it is, you look at it right now, you're getting a salary every week. You don't know how long you're going to last.

It might go to where your job's going down, your clothes, anything. So they have to continue with it. Can you play any jazz? Can you play any blues at this job you have? Yeah we play whatever you want. They don't care what you play down there, they only want you to play.

They play anything. We play blues, jazz, swing, concerts, waltzes, anything. Nobody cares, huh? They don't care what you play. They had some jobs, one night before they had the piccolo in there, on the rest grid that used to turn the radio off. I'm trying to watch some of the guys like music, when they have the news, you have news like 11 o'clock news, and the guys keep on dancing, you know, just keep on dancing. That's not like a joke, but it's not. That's a good boy. That must make you feel good. They didn't need it. They don't want to dance. They didn't answer those girls. That's what I said, we play anything down there. Well it's true except sometimes somebody comes with me and plays a couple of dollars and plays some so on.
They used to have all those in New Orleans too. A lot of good old time musicians used to work there, but now they've all gone with the jazz concerts I guess.

They're all. They used to be there in China, a dozen, and more in New York. But this is the only one that has live music. Only one with live music? Yeah. I guess I've worked at least a half a dozen more, or maybe more than around New York since I've been there. But it's the only one that's with live music. Did they have places like that in New Orleans in the old days? I didn't even know if I knew of them. I never knew of them until I came to New York. I never heard of a dance school until I got to go. They called them dance school, but they're taxi dance hall. I think they called them jitneys too.
Yeah. I don't know, is that the same thing that you ever used that word?

I don't know, I don't know, it used to be five cents a dance, they gave me, that's what they call it jit dance, ten cents a dance. Really they were supposed to be ten cents a dance. But everything's gone up, so they're gone up too, twenty-five cents a dance. Twenty-five cents. They don't advertise, they just have four tickets for a dollar. So they got some work. Ain't no more dance hall in New York. You take it for a dance hall, it used to be three or four dance halls, what they call ballroom, they don't have that in New York. The pay is so high, they cost so much to pay a band. They get around with an old band, I guess, about the only ballroom to go in New York now. I think one of the 50th or 30th, they were supposed to be really open. But they can't afford it. The price is high, the rent is high, everything else is high.
See, one thing I wanted to ask you before I forget, how about the blues singers? You made records with some of the blues singers. I made quite a few of them.

Tooth Smith, Clarence Smith, Sarah Morton. I can't remember one of them. See, Clarence just recorded all those blues singers. So I used to go over there and play behind them. I made records, Jess Trumpet. Did you ever record with Ida Cox? No, I never recorded with Ida Cox. But you heard of her, huh? Yeah. She used to be in New York. But she's supposed to be coming back. That's good. I always see somebody get some money. I can't even think of all those blues singers. I mean, somebody, when you look in there, I told you about the blues singers coming to New York, I ain't loving it. I mean, many records, yeah.
What was the first time you played that style to a company of blues singers? Did you ever play any of that kind of music in St. Louis? In New Orleans or anything?
No, I think it was my first game there. New York.
You just picked it up.

Did anybody teach it to you? No. Each one have an individual style, you know. You play something that sounds good. And I played them with Clarence, he liked that. So if I play something else, he scored. I used to play some sweet melody with me playing, Clarence. Come on, cuz. They don't want to hear that. Give me some quack, quack, quack, quack. You like that, man. Come on, quack, quack. That ain't like listening to that. That ain't you. Play some quack, quack, quack, quack. I used to get some quack, quack, quack. I used to get some quack, quack, quack. I used to get some quack, quack, quack. Why do you want to make these records now? They got to play what they want. They don't want to hear you play sweet. What was that you were telling me about the time you made a record and the people who
had the comedy said it was too sweet? Yeah.
I forget the metal, they were beautiful. They called us back and said they want that style music out. I wasn't expecting that. They were going to make it all over.
They think a colored band should play rough right now?
Mm-hmm. Blues. Sounds like that. It was a popular number, I don't remember this, like years ago, a popular number. Even Clapper said he doesn't want to hear that sound.

He said, I think that's something. He said, listen to this record. They want you to make it over. I don't know. I said, what's wrong with it? He said, that's what I want to know. What's wrong with it? They said it was too smooth or too sweet or something. Well we heard you play some sweet stuff on some of those old records. That's what I know. But this particular record didn't want it. I think most of them was a popular number.

I thought they really made me a popular number, very subtle. Especially the washboard records, those, some blue fires that they had. They were all originals, huh? Yeah. That's what they wanted. I guess they didn't want to pay royalties or something. Well Clarence probably wanted a copyright. Yeah. They had to pay royalties.

Anybody put their name on it. I don't know how they got around that. Well he's got a lot of numbers in his name that I'm sure he didn't write. I think so too. A lot of people coming in, having them stacked up on the shelf.

I'm afraid of different people going to go, man, where are you going to put that number up? Well I'm a time not right for it now. I got something in the head of you. And someone in the head of you and someone in the head of you and someone in the head of the head of the head of the head of the head of the head of the head of the head of the head of the head of the head of the head of the head of the head of the head of the head

segments.title: Opening: date, location and Ed Allen's birth
segments.summary: Interviewer opens the session and confirms Allen was born in Nashville in December 1897.

segments.title: Kid band, bugle, and Professor Blue's lessons in St. Louis
segments.summary: Allen's mother played ear piano; he quit piano for a kid military band, started on bugle and trumpet, learned to read under Professor Blue, and played dances and roadhouses.

segments.title: Day jobs, marriage and leaving St. Louis for Seattle
segments.summary: Before leaving in 1920 he worked in a foundry and packing house, played nightclubs a few nights a week, then took a $50 a week job on the coast.

segments.title: Streckfus riverboat job and forming the Gold Whistler band
segments.summary: Back in St. Louis he played the day excursion boat, and the boat owner picked him to lead a band of St. Louis and New Orleans players for the New Orleans run.

segments.title: The ten-piece boat band: sound, head arrangements and success
segments.summary: Allen describes the three reed, three brass, four rhythm band, its head arrangements, a New Orleans standard that rocked the boat, and its success in New Orleans and St. Louis.

segments.title: New Orleans trumpeters and Floyd Casey
segments.summary: Allen recalls Kid Punch and other New Orleans players and his drummer Floyd Casey.

segments.title: Hearing Oliver and Armstrong; comparison of styles
segments.summary: He heard Oliver and Armstrong in St. Louis, later played with Oliver in New York, and discusses whether his style resembled Oliver's.

segments.title: Taking the New Orleans nightclub job after the boat band
segments.summary: After the band split, Allen took a $40 a week nightclub job offered by the owner Butchie.

segments.title: Slipping away from the club; the owner turns up in New York
segments.summary: Allen recalls the small band, how he left for St. Louis, and the owner finding him at Connie's Inn in New York.

segments.title: New Orleans bands: Celestin and Manuel Perez
segments.summary: Allen and the interviewer discuss Celestin's and Manuel Perez's bands and that he met Piron only in New York.

segments.chapter: Chicago, burlesque show and New York
segments.title: Piron and meeting Clarence Williams in New York
segments.summary: Allen met Piron and Clarence Williams only in New York, through Jasper Taylor, and got recording work.

segments.chapter: Chicago, burlesque show and New York
segments.title: Chicago, Earl Hines, Joe Jordan and the burlesque show to New York
segments.summary: Allen worked in Chicago, met Earl Hines, joined Joe Jordan's burlesque show band for two years, then settled in New York recording for Clarence Williams.

segments.title: Clarence Williams: songs, publishing and record dates
segments.summary: Williams made up songs overnight, used lead sheets, ran a publishing house, and Allen recalls a Bluebird record and sidemen on the dates.

segments.title: Clarence Williams today: royalties, health, wife and son
segments.summary: Talk of Williams's Decca royalties, his illness, thrift shop, son, and his singer wife.

segments.title: Sessions: who was hired and how they ran
segments.summary: Williams drew players from across New York; sessions were rushed, with last-minute changes and a week of catalog recording.

segments.title: King Oliver and Williams's blues-contest recordings
segments.summary: Oliver sometimes recorded with Williams; Williams hired trumpeters for blues contest winners and chose men by results; Allen names the bands he worked with.

segments.title: Origins of the washboard band
segments.summary: Allen credits Jasper Taylor, then Floyd Casey, with the washboard; discusses its use on records and in the burlesque show.

segments.title: Connie's Inn, the Cotton Club, Fletcher Henderson and freelancing
segments.summary: Connie's Inn and the Cotton Club were top Harlem spots in 1927-28; Allen never played with Henderson, and freelanced after Connie's.

segments.title: New Orleans musicians in New York and Louis Armstrong
segments.summary: Brief exchange about New Orleans players in New York and Allen's admiration for Armstrong.

segments.title: Charlie Creath, St. Louis trumpeter
segments.summary: Allen praises Charlie Creath's tone and blues playing, his bands around St. Louis, the Zutty Singleton family tie, and his death.

segments.title: Chicago trumpeters and New Orleans men in New York
segments.summary: Allen was in Chicago only about three months and knew few musicians there or New Orleans men in New York.

segments.title: Freelancing and the dance school job: fatigue and ticket dancing
segments.summary: Allen describes gigging with different bands and a current taxi dance hall job: tiring four-piece nights, slow numbers, and tickets four for a dollar.

segments.title: Dance school band: Rudy Powell, Floyd Casey and the rotating schedule
segments.summary: Allen speaks of Rudy Powell and the band's nightly rotation of players, and the ages of the musicians.

segments.title: Work for older musicians in New York and the end of dance halls
segments.summary: Steady jobs are few, they play anything at the dance school, taxi dance halls were unknown in New Orleans, and ballrooms have closed.

segments.title: Playing behind blues singers for Williams
segments.summary: Allen backed many blues singers on Williams's dates, learned the style in New York, and was told to play rough rather than sweet.

segments.title: Records rejected as too sweet and publishing practices
segments.summary: A record was sent back as too smooth, and Allen and the interviewer discuss Williams's copyrights and publishers shelving numbers.

segments.title: Rock and roll and Dixieland demand
segments.summary: Allen says his band plays rock and roll when paid, and notes demand for Dixieland; the transcript degrades into a loop.

segments.title: Getting work through cliques in New York
segments.summary: Allen says jobs depend on who you know, contrasting the 1920s, then the transcript ends in an ASR loop.
